Toucan seen flying around Las Vegas has been rescued
LAS VEGAS (AP) — A toucan that has been seen flying around Las Vegas for months has been saved, a bird rescue group said Wednesday.
“We’ve all just been so worried about him,” said Skye Marsh, the president and co-founder of the SouthWest Exotic Avian Rescue. “It’s a relief.”
Sam the toucan has been living in Las Vegas since November, much to the concern of bird experts and enthusiasts who were worried about the exotic bird’s health and his ability to survive long-term in a city with drastic weather changes.
“(The) little stinker decided it was time for help, and he flew into someone’s garage,” Skye told The Associated Press. The homeowners knew who the toucan was and shut the garage so he couldn’t escape. Sam has captivated the Las Vegas community after surviving in the desert for months.
After the rescue group caught him, staff took him to a local veterinarian. There are some signs of “wear and tear,” such as dehydrated skin and a chip off his beak, but he seems to be OK, Skye said. The veterinarian gave him fluids and took bloodwork.
Sam had been eating better food since the rescue group put out healthier toucan food around a cage to try to rescue him. Skye said the better food improved his health, as his poop was looking healthier leading up to his rescue.
Sam’s owners, who had posted on social media about the bird’s escape from its cage in November, has not been in contact with the rescue group.
The toucan will be in quarantine at a staff member’s house for 30 to 45 days to make sure he does not have bird flu, which spreads to other birds at the rescue, Skye said.

Toucan seen flying around Las Vegas is rescued after surviving in desert for months
A toucan that has been seen flying around Las Vegas for months has been saved, a bird rescue group said Wednesday.
"We've all just been so worried about him," said Skye Marsh, the president and co-founder of the SouthWest Exotic Avian Rescue (SWEAR). "It's a relief."
"Sam is found!" the group wrote on social media on Wednesday.
Sam the toucan has been living in Las Vegas since November, much to the concern of bird experts and enthusiasts who were worried about the exotic bird's health and his ability to survive long-term in a city with drastic weather changes.
"(The) little stinker decided it was time for help, and he flew into someone's garage," Marsh told The Associated Press. The homeowners knew who the toucan was and shut the garage so he couldn't escape. Sam has captivated the Las Vegas community after surviving in the desert for months.
After the rescue group caught him, staff took him to a local veterinarian. There are some signs of "wear and tear," such as dehydrated skin and a chip off his beak, but he seems to be OK, Marsh said. The veterinarian gave him fluids and took bloodwork.
Sam had been eating better food since the rescue group put out healthier toucan food around a cage to try to rescue him. Marsh said the better food improved his health, as his poop was looking healthier leading up to his rescue.
Sam's owners, who had posted on social media about the bird's escape from its cage in November, has not been in contact with the rescue group.
The toucan will be in quarantine at a staff member's house for 30 to 45 days to make sure he does not have bird flu, which spreads to other birds at the rescue, Marsh said.
According to the San Diego Zoo, toucans typically spend their lives high in the rainforest canopies of Central and South America. They are primarily frugivores but are also known to eat insects, tree frogs and lizards.
Marsh told the Las Vegas Review-Journal that Sam likely lived off figs and pomegranates from trees after he first escaped, and later ate citrus, which can be harmful to the birds.
Marsh believes the bird was as happy as the rescue group that he was saved.
"I think he was a little bit relieved," Marsh told the Las Vegas Review-Journal. "I think he was done doing the free bird thing."

Lost toucan is found: Tropical bird seen flying around Las Vegas rescued
Since mid-November, bird enthusiast Skye Marsh of Las Vegas had been hoping to get the call she received Wednesday afternoon.
The lost toucan, appropriately named Sam, had been found.
“I got a call from a member of the public who had been following the story about Sam being lost,” Marsh said. “They said Sam had flown into their garage and that they had him trapped.”
The toucan, which had been seen soaring around the west side of the Las Vegas Valley for months,flew into a garage at a home in northwest Las Vegas near Lone Mountain and Fort Apache roads on Wednesday. The homeowner, who had been aware of the loose toucan, quickly shut their garage door and prevented the bird from leaving, Marsh said.
Within minutes, Marsh said, multiple members of the board from the Las Vegas-based SouthWest Exotic Avian Rescue, which she helps run, were at the home.
“I’m sure it was a little bit funny to watch all of us trying to catch something that flies like a dream, but we did get him and I think he was a little bit relieved,” Marsh said. “I think he was done doing the free bird thing.”
Health check
Soon after, Marsh said, Sam was in the care of Dr. Anne Beckes, an associate veterinarian at Aloha Animal Hospital. He was dehydrated, Marsh said, and had some feathers missing on his head, but he was in one piece.
On Wednesday afternoon, Sam was in a cage in Marsh’s backyard. As he hopped from one side of the cage to the other, and back again, Marsh said the bird appeared to still be stressed. She said it was a relief to have finally found him.
Being a toucan, a tropical bird, Sam’s preferred climate is a lot less dry than Las Vegas. Toucans are native to rain forests in Central and South America.
While Sam was on the lam, Marsh said there were also concerns about predators — think something like a red-tailed hawk — and malnutrition since birds like Sam like to eat fruit.
“Their main diet is primarily going to be papayas or cantaloupe,” said Kim Bauer-Schaub of the rescue group. “They’ll also supplement with other fruits.”
Donald Price, a professor and biologist at UNLV who studies how winged animal species adapt to different environments, said a desert is not a good environment for a bird like Sam.
“For him to be out as long as he was, we were getting really worried,” Marsh said. “I’ve lost a lot of sleep over this.”
As Marsh talked, she gestured behind her at the 4-foot cage that housed the troublesome toucan.
“This kid owes me a touch-up on my roots because I’ve gotten quite a few more silver hairs because of him,” Marsh said.
The chase
Marsh said Sam’s owner posted on social media about the bird’s escape from its cage in the area of the Los Prados neighborhood in the northwest valley November, though the owner hasn’t been heard from since. Marsh said she tried to contact the owner but was unsuccessful. Members of birding groups and others posted periodically to social media sites if they noticed Sam around town.
Marsh, who has two toucans of her own, said Sam will be in quarantine at a private home in Las Vegas for up to 45 days to sure he doesn’t have bird flu. Marsh said that she’s not thinking about a new forever home for Sam just yet.
“Right now, I’m only thinking about two days into the future,” Marsh said. “We’re waiting on results from the vet on some blood work. For now, he has to be in quarantine because he’s been exposed to wild birds.”
Marsh and others with SouthWest Exotic Avian Rescue suspect that Sam’s previous owner likely hadn’t cared for the bird — which can fetch thousands of dollars on the open market — properly.
Marsh believes Sam likely lived off figs and pomegranates from trees in the area of the Los Prados neighborhood after he first escaped. She said he likely later graduated to citrus, which can be harmful to toucans.
Members of the rescue group set up a cage with food to try to entice Sam, but that didn’t work, Marsh said.
“Toucans, it’s just an absolutely beautiful bird to look at,” Marsh said. “They all have their own little personalities and they’re very smart, almost like a toddler. They’re really neat birds, but you have to have the right environment for a toucan. It’s a huge, huge relief to have him.”
Contact Bryan Horwath at bhorwath@reviewjournal.com. Follow @BryanHorwath on X. The Associated Press contributed to this report.
